title: Why (Senior) Engineers Struggle to Build AI Agents — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
talk_summary: Philipp Schmid argues agent engineering differs from traditional software: define goals and context, treat errors as inputs, evaluate pass rates rather than deterministic tests, and design agent-ready tools. He recommends trusting models with recovery and outcome-based verification instead of forcing rigid workflows.

takeaways.technique: Pass-rate eval harness instead of unit-test assertions
takeaways.what_they_do: They replace deterministic unit-test assumptions with eval suites that measure how often a non-deterministic agent succeeds across repeated runs, using LLM judges or human experts and tracing outcomes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need to move from unit tests to eval. We need to test how often something works

takeaways.technique: Errors as model-visible inputs with recovery
takeaways.what_they_do: They treat tool/API failures as normal inputs to the model and preserve context so long agent runs can continue or recover instead of restarting from scratch.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if something in your agent flow fails, we need to treat it as a normal input

takeaways.what_they_do: They design APIs/tools for agents with self-documenting semantic interfaces, examples, and failure semantics because agents only see function schemas and docstrings.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agents only see like the function schemas and the doc strings and the tool definition

takeaways.what_they_do: They use natural-language context as state for plans, memory, and preferences, allowing nuanced approve-with-additional-instructions instead of rigid boolean flags.
They define the goal and constraints and let the model choose steps, while verifying outcomes rather than forcing one exact workflow.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We should stop fighting the model. You should not like try to force the model into this one specific workflow

takeaways.technique: Disposable model adapters plus eval gate
takeaways.what_they_do: They expect prompts and tools to be rebuilt as models improve, treating software as disposable and verifying swaps by outcome.
takeaways.evidence_quote: software is disposable. We are going to rebuild many, many times the same things with better models
